text: Every lesson since Lesson 1 has been building toward this moment. Priya's real question was never do we have backups — it was has anyone actually restored one. This lesson is where that question finally gets a real, tested answer.

If you've seen on-prem SQL Server restores, you know the chained pattern: restore the full with NORECOVERY, restore the differential with NORECOVERY, restore each log backup in order, and only the final one with RECOVERY to bring the database online. Azure SQL Database replaces that entire manual sequence with one operation. You pick a target database and a timestamp, and Azure selects the right full, the right differential, and every log backup needed, applying them in the correct order automatically. That chained logic doesn't disappear — Azure is doing exactly that internally. It's just no longer something you orchestrate by hand.

From the Portal, the Restore button lets you choose point in time, pick a timestamp, and give the restored copy a new name. From the CLI, it's one command: az sql db restore, with a destination name and a target time in UTC. Either way, Azure provisions a new database and assembles the full-plus-differential-plus-log chain automatically, finishing in minutes.

Here's the detail worth sitting with. The restore never touches the original database — it produces an entirely separate one alongside it. That's the safer design, not a limitation. In a real incident, you restore, verify the copy actually has what you expect — row counts, a spot-check of recent records — and only then decide how to use it: swap connection strings, or copy specific data back into the original.

That's the restore, actually performed and verified — the single most important lab in this whole project. Next lesson, you'll write a simple, real query that confirms the database is healthy right now, any time you want to check.
